# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Everyday decisions are often made while the body is working, yet little is known about how physical effort changes decision-making in older adults. Physical effort could degrade the quality of the evidence on which a decision is based, change how much evidence people require before committing to a response (response caution), or bias them toward one response. We tested these accounts in `r v("n_final")` older adults who judged whether two tones, or two visual gratings, were the same or different while squeezing a handgrip at 5% (low physical effort) or 40% (high physical effort) of their maximum force. Pupil size was recorded throughout. Choices and response times were analyzed with a hierarchical Bayesian drift-diffusion model, which separates evidence quality, response caution and the starting point, a bias toward one response set before the stimulus appears. High physical effort did not reduce evidence quality overall, and any additional cost on the hardest discriminations was small. Instead, it produced a small shift in the criterion against which evidence was evaluated toward "same" responses on every trial, which lowered accuracy when two similar stimuli differed. Response caution and the starting point were essentially unchanged. High physical effort enlarged the pupil only weakly during the grip, reliably in the auditory task alone. Larger pupil responses during a decision accompanied greater response caution on that trial, but pupil size measured before the decision did not predict caution. Physical effort therefore mainly changed the criterion older adults used to evaluate evidence, not the quality of that evidence.

# 1 Introduction {.unnumbered}

Many everyday decisions are made while the body is working, such as judging a gap in traffic while gripping a steering wheel or reading a label while carrying groceries. Combining a cognitive task with a motor task costs older adults more than younger adults [@verhaeghen2003], and sustained isometric force is one such motor demand: an effortful handgrip impairs cognitive control and working memory in later life [@azer2023]. Accuracy and response time (RT) show that performance suffers, but not which part of the decision process changes.

Chapter 1 [@dastgheib_inpress_effects] used the same 5% and 40% handgrip levels in younger adults performing a working-memory task and two discrimination tasks, one auditory and one visual. Harder trials were less accurate in every task and slower in both discrimination tasks, high physical effort slowed responses only in the visual discrimination task, and task difficulty and physical effort did not interact on any measure. High physical effort also enlarged the pupil across the trial. In younger adults, physical effort and task difficulty therefore appeared to draw on separate resources. Chapter 2 then showed, in the present sample, that high physical effort lowered "different" responses without reducing sensitivity. On trials with identical stimuli the reduction was of similar size but uncertain on its own. Choices alone cannot tell whether this reflects a shifted criterion, a change in how much evidence participants required, or a bias set before the stimulus; separating these requires RTs. This chapter uses both to answer that question.

The drift-diffusion model decomposes choices and RTs into latent components [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. It treats a two-choice decision as noisy evidence that accumulates until it reaches one of two boundaries (@fig-design, panel B). Drift rate (*v*) is the average direction and speed of accumulation; boundary separation (*a*) is how much evidence is required before responding, and so indexes response caution; the starting point (*z*) is a bias toward one response before the stimulus appears; and non-decision time (*t*~0~) covers encoding and response execution. Lower accuracy can therefore arise from less informative evidence, from responding on less evidence, or from a bias toward the wrong response. In older adults, the most consistent age differences are wider boundaries and longer non-decision times, whereas drift is often similar to that of younger adults on simple perceptual tasks [@ratcliff2001aging; @theisen2021age], and older adults set boundaries more conservatively than would maximize their reward rate [@starns2010effects]. Response caution is therefore a plausible target of physical effort in this age group, alongside evidence quality.

A capacity account holds that physical effort competes with the judgment for a limited pool of processing resources [@kahneman1973attention; @wickens2008]. On each trial, participants judged whether a probe matched a preceding standard. If holding a 40% grip draws on the resources needed for that comparison, the evidence should become less informative: drift on trials with a different probe should move closer to drift on trials with an identical one. Because a shared limit should cost most where discrimination is hardest, this loss of evidence quality should be largest on the hardest trials, producing an interaction between physical effort and task difficulty.

A policy account holds instead that physical effort changes how participants use the evidence, not the evidence itself. Participants could require more evidence before responding, to protect accuracy, which would widen the boundaries. Alternatively, they could require less, to end each effortful trial sooner, which would narrow them. Physical effort could also bias responding toward "same" or "different." A bias set before the stimulus appears would move the starting point. A bias in how the evidence is evaluated would instead shift the drift criterion, the reference against which evidence counts as favoring one response [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. Such a shift moves drift toward one response on every trial, so it can lower accuracy on difficult trials with a different probe even when evidence quality is intact. Distinguishing the two accounts therefore requires estimating the criterion and evidence quality separately.

Pupil size offers a trial-by-trial physiological measure relevant to both accounts. It increases with task difficulty [@beatty1982; @vanderwel2018pupil] and with physical effort [@zenon2014pupil], although older adults have smaller pupils and a narrower range of dilation than younger adults [@winn1994factors; @piquado2010pupillometry]. In diffusion-model analyses, larger trial-wise pupil dilation has been related to wider boundaries in a reinforcement-learning task [@cavanagh2014] and to smaller choice biases across several decision tasks [@degee2020pupil]. Pupil responses, however, also increase with decision uncertainty and RT [@urai2017], so a pupil–boundary association could arise simply because longer decisions produce larger pupil responses. Testing whether pupil-linked processes precede the setting of the boundary requires pupil measures taken before the decision, as well as measures that end before the response.

We tested these accounts in older adults performing auditory and visual same–different tasks while holding a handgrip at 5% or 40% of their maximum force. A hierarchical Bayesian drift-diffusion model estimated the effect of physical effort on each decision component. The capacity account predicts a loss of evidence quality under high physical effort that is largest on the hardest trials. The policy account predicts a change in boundary separation, starting point or drift criterion, with evidence quality intact. Trial-wise pupil measures were then added to the same model to test whether pupil size tracked the physical effort effect, which decision component tracked the task-evoked pupil response, and whether pupil measures taken before the decision predicted boundary separation.

# 2 Methods {.unnumbered}

## 2.1 Participants {.unnumbered}

Community-dwelling adults aged 60–90 years were recruited around the University of California, Riverside. All were right-handed, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing, and had no contraindication for MRI, no current psychotropic medication, no neurological disorder and no major systemic condition (including diabetes). Of `r v("n_enrolled")` enrolled participants, `r nw(v("n_excluded"))` were excluded (suspected mild cognitive impairment; possible essential tremor). That left `r v("n_final")` older adults (@tbl-demographics). Choices and confidence in this cohort were analyzed by @sun2026handgrip and, at the level of trials, in Chapter 2. Under the inclusion criteria, `r v("n_adt") + v("n_vdt") - v("n_final")` participants contributed data to both tasks and `r nw(2 * v("n_final") - v("n_adt") - v("n_vdt"))` to only one (auditory, `r v("n_adt")`; visual, `r v("n_vdt")`). Participants gave written informed consent and received payment. Procedures were approved by the University of California, Riverside Institutional Review Board.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-demographics
#| tbl-cap: "Participant characteristics"
ch3_tbl_demographics(tbl$T1_demographics)
```

## 2.2 Task, stimuli and sessions {.unnumbered}

Participants performed an auditory discrimination task (ADT) and a visual discrimination task (VDT) in the MRI scanner while squeezing a dynamometer with the left hand (@fig-design, panel A). After a blank gray screen (1.5–4.5 s), a grip gauge appeared for 3 s with a target at 5% (low physical effort) or 40% (high physical effort) of the participant's maximum voluntary contraction (MVC). Participants held the grip until probe offset, when a change in the border color cued them to release it. After a 0.25-s blank and a 0.5-s fixation dot, a standard and a comparison stimulus (the probe; called the target in Chapter 1), each 0.1 s long, were presented 0.5 s apart. In the ADT, the standard was a 1000-Hz tone, and the probe was identical or 8, 16, 32 or 64 Hz higher. In the VDT, the standard was a Gabor patch (1.5 cycles/degree, Michelson contrast 0.20, 4°), and the probe was identical or had a contrast 0.06, 0.12, 0.24 or 0.48 higher. The two smaller offsets were grouped as Hard, the two larger as Easy, and trials with an identical probe as Identical (the catch trials of Chapter 2).

Responses were delayed: participants withheld their response until a cue appeared 0.25 s after probe offset. They then had 3 s to answer "different" (right index finger) or "same" (right middle finger), followed by a confidence rating that is not analyzed here. Each task had five blocks of 30 trials. Each block crossed the five probe levels with the two physical effort levels, three times each, in pseudorandom order. Physical effort was therefore known before each trial, but the stimulus type was known only at probe onset.

```{r}
#| label: fig-design
#| fig-cap: !expr cap_fig_design()
#| out-width: "100%"
suppressWarnings(knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath(file.path(params$figures_dir, "F1_design_model.png"), mustWork = TRUE), error = FALSE))
```

The tasks were completed across three sessions on separate days. In Session 1, participants watched instructional videos and practiced at least 60 trials of each task without the grip, and their MVC was measured. They then practiced both tasks with the grip and confidence ratings until the experimenter judged that they understood them. In Sessions 2 and 3, participants performed one task each in the scanner (order counterbalanced), each preceded by a short practice block. MVC was the mean force across three maximal 5-s squeezes, with about 30 s of rest between them. It was measured again in the scanner in Session 2, and that value set the 5% and 40% targets in Sessions 2 and 3.

## 2.3 Apparatus {.unnumbered}

The task ran in Psychophysics Toolbox 3.0.18 [@brainard1997psychophysics; @kleiner2007s] in MATLAB R2022b. Visual stimuli were projected with a PROPixx projector (VPixx Technologies; 480 Hz, 1920 × 1080) and viewed through a head-coil mirror (effective viewing distance 12 cm). Sounds were delivered through MRI-compatible earbuds (Newmatic Medical; 30 dB noise reduction). Responses were recorded with a RESPONSEpixx button box, grip force with an MRI-compatible dynamometer (Current Designs; 100 Hz) and pupil diameter with a TRACKPixx binocular eye tracker (VPixx Technologies; 2000 Hz). The background was mid-gray. The gauge's force bar covered less than 1% of the screen, so it changed mean luminance by less than 1% between physical effort levels, in the direction that would constrict the pupil under high physical effort.

## 2.4 Behavioral data processing {.unnumbered}

RT was recorded from the response cue. For modeling it was measured from probe onset, by adding the fixed 0.35-s interval between probe onset and the cue, so that the decision clock starts when evidence becomes available and the non-decision time absorbs the enforced delay. Of `r fmt_int(v("n_trials_raw"))` recorded trials, `r nw(v("n_trials_negative_rt"))` with a negative RT were removed. A further `r fmt_int(v("n_trials_cutoff_excluded"))` with a cue-locked RT below 0.20 s were removed as anticipatory. This left `r fmt_int(v("n_trials_primary"))` trials (@supptbl-trial-counts). Cutoffs of 0.15 s and 0.25 s were used in sensitivity analyses. Overall accuracy was at or below .55 for `r v("n_subchance_excluded")` participants. They were retained in the primary analysis and excluded in a sensitivity analysis.

## 2.5 Pupillometry {.unnumbered}

Blinks and other artifacts were removed with the ET-remove-artifacts toolbox [@mather2020isometric] and checked visually. The signal was downsampled to 250 Hz, and each sample was placed on a time axis at 4-ms steps from 3 s before squeeze onset. This axis spans the recorded epoch, which ends with the confidence window 10.7 s after squeeze onset.

The task-evoked pupil response (TEPR) was the mean pupil size 0.3–3.3 s after probe onset (4.65–7.65 s after squeeze onset) minus the mean pupil size in the 0.5 s before the probe (3.85–4.35 s, the interstimulus interval). As in Chapter 1, this baseline separates the response to the probe from the slower dilation that builds up during the grip. The window starts 0.3 s after the probe to allow for pupil latency [@mathot2018] and covers the typical peak, 1–2 s after the stimulus [@dasilvacastanheira2021task]. Because the window extends past the response on most trials, the TEPR includes post-decision processing; Section 2.7 describes how this was tested. Two further measures were the mean pupil size in the 0.5 s before squeeze onset (pre-squeeze baseline) and the mean pupil size during the grip (`r fmt_num(v("grip_window_start"), 2)`–`r fmt_num(v("grip_window_end"), 2)` s), relative to the pre-squeeze baseline.

Trials entered the pupil analyses if at least 50% of samples were valid in both the pre-probe baseline and the TEPR window. Each participant × task cell needed at least 20 such trials. This left `r fmt_int(v("n_pupil_final_trials"))` trials from `r v("n_pupil_final_subjects")` participants (@suppfig-flow), a subset of the behavioral sample selected on recording quality. Each pupil predictor was centered within participant × task × physical effort and divided by the participant's pooled within-cell SD. Its slope therefore reflects trial-to-trial fluctuation around the condition mean.

## 2.6 Drift-diffusion model {.unnumbered}

Choices and probe-locked RTs were modeled with a Wiener diffusion model [@ratcliff2008diffusion], with "different" as the upper boundary and "same" as the lower boundary. Positive drift therefore moves toward "different." The starting point measures a bias toward one response. On Identical trials, drift is negative when evidence accumulates toward the correct "same" response.

Models were fit jointly to both tasks in brms [@burkner2017brms] with CmdStan [@cmdstan2024], using an identity link for drift, log links for boundary separation (*a*) and non-decision time (*t*~0~), and a logit link for the starting point (*z*). In the primary model (M4; @fig-design, panel C), drift depended on stimulus type (Identical, Hard, Easy), task (ADT, VDT), a stimulus type × task interaction, physical effort (low, high) and a physical effort × stimulus term; boundary separation depended on stimulus type, task and physical effort; the starting point depended on task and physical effort; and non-decision time had an intercept only. Identical trials, the ADT and low physical effort were the reference levels. Because the response cue was a fixed delay, non-decision time absorbed that delay, and physical effort effects on it were not tested. Participants had random intercepts on drift, boundary separation and starting point.

The model terms map onto the two accounts. The physical effort main effect on drift shifts drift equally on all trials, toward "different" if positive and toward "same" if negative, a change in the drift criterion [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. The physical effort × stimulus term (stimulus coded +1 for Hard and Easy, −1 for Identical) changes how far drift on trials with a different probe lies from drift on Identical trials, a change in evidence quality. To test whether a loss of evidence quality was largest on the hardest trials, a model in which the physical effort effects varied with task difficulty (M2) was compared with the same model without that interaction (M1). The physical effort effects on boundary separation and on the starting point test the remaining predictions of the policy account. Model selection, robustness variants and formulas are described in the supplement (@sec-supp-spec).

Priors were weakly informative on the link scale (@supptbl-priors). Models used `r v("n_chains")` chains of `r fmt_int(v("n_iter"))` iterations, the first `r fmt_int(v("n_warmup"))` of them warmup. A model was accepted if every parameter had R̂ < 1.01, bulk and tail effective sample sizes of at least 400 and no divergent transitions [@vehtari2021rank]. @supptbl-convergence gives the diagnostics for every model.

## 2.7 Pupil-linked models {.unnumbered}

Each pupil-linked model added one pupil predictor to the primary model and was compared with the primary model fit to the same trials. To test which decision component tracked the TEPR, the TEPR was entered on the starting point (P1), on drift with a TEPR × stimulus term (P2) or on boundary separation (P3). To test whether pupil measures taken before the decision predicted boundary separation, the pre-squeeze baseline (P5), the grip-period pupil size (P8) and the previous trial's TEPR within a block (P6) were each entered on boundary separation, and the pre-squeeze baseline was also entered on the starting point (P4). Because the TEPR window overlapped the response, a TEPR–boundary association could reflect decision duration rather than a pupil change before the decision. To test this, P3 was refit without the slowest 20% of trials in each participant × task cell, and pupil size in the 0.5 s before the response was entered on boundary separation (P7).

Physical effort effects on pupil size were tested with paired *t* tests on participant means within each task, with the TEPR compared relative to both the pre-probe and the pre-squeeze baseline. Only participants with valid trials at both physical effort levels were included.

## 2.8 Statistical inference {.unnumbered}

Each effect is summarized by the median of its posterior distribution and a 95% credible interval (CrI), the range that contains the effect with 95% probability given the data and model. We also report the posterior probability that the effect has the sign of its median, for example P(β < 0), which can be read directly as the probability that the effect is negative. To decide whether an effect was negligible rather than merely uncertain, we defined a region of practical equivalence [ROPE, @kruschke2018rejecting], a range of values too small to matter; the more of the posterior that falls inside it, the stronger the evidence that the effect is negligible. The ROPE was ±`r fmt_num(v("rope_a"), 2)` for log boundary separation and logit starting point, about a 5% change in *a* and about 1 percentage point in *z* near its observed value, and ±`r fmt_num(v("rope_v"), 2)` for drift, about 1% of the drift difference between Identical and Easy trials. Bayes factors were not computed because, for effects in a hierarchical diffusion model, they depend strongly on the width of the prior on each effect, and the priors here were weakly informative rather than chosen to represent specific alternative hypotheses [@kruschke2018rejecting].

Models were compared by how well they predicted trials they had not been fitted to, using leave-one-out cross-validation [PSIS-LOO, @vehtari2017practical]. The comparison is a difference in expected log predictive density (ΔELPD), which is positive when the model with the added term predicts better. It is reported with its SE, and differences smaller than about twice their SE were treated as uncertain.

Observed accuracy was analyzed with a binomial generalized linear mixed model (stimulus type × physical effort, plus task) in lme4 [@bates2015lme4]. Because models with random physical effort slopes were singular, the model used a random intercept for participant [@barr2013maximal; @bates2015parsimonious; @brauer2018lmm]. High − Low contrasts at each stimulus type were computed with emmeans [@lenth2024emmeans]. Model adequacy was checked by simulating choices and RTs from the fitted model and comparing them with the observed choice proportions and RT quantiles in each of the 12 task × stimulus type × physical effort cells.

# 3 Results {.unnumbered}

## 3.1 Primary diffusion model {.unnumbered}

**Stimulus and task effects.** Drift was negative on Identical and Hard trials and positive on Easy trials (@fig-condition-params; @supptbl-condition-cells), so that on Hard trials evidence on average favored "same" although the probe differed (low physical effort; ADT: `r cell_s("v_cell_ADT_Hard")`; VDT: `r cell_s("v_cell_VDT_Hard")`). In both tasks the starting point lay above 0.5, toward the "different" boundary (ADT: *z* = `r prob_s("z_ADT")`; VDT: *z* = `r prob_s("z_VDT")`). Differences between stimulus types and tasks in drift and boundary separation are given in @supptbl-fixef-m4.


```{r}
#| label: fig-condition-params
#| fig-cap: !expr cap_fig_condition_params()
#| out-width: "100%"
suppressWarnings(knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath(file.path(params$figures_dir, "F2_condition_parameters.png"), mustWork = TRUE), error = FALSE))
```

**Physical effort effects.** High physical effort shifted drift toward "same" on all trials (drift criterion: `r eff("crit")`; @fig-effort-forest; @tbl-effort-effects). The physical effort × stimulus term, which indexes evidence quality, was close to zero (`r eff("qual")`). Drift decreased on trials with a different probe (`r eff("drift_diff_trials")`); on Identical trials the change was smaller, and its interval included zero (`r eff("drift_same_trials")`). Allowing the physical effort effects on drift and boundary separation to vary with task difficulty did not improve prediction (`r elpd_s("delta_elpd_M2_vs_M1", "se_delta_elpd_M2_vs_M1")`; @supptbl-model-comparison). In that model, the physical effort effect on drift was more negative on Hard than on Easy trials (Hard − Easy: `r eff("m2_v_hard_minus_easy_x_high")`), whereas the corresponding contrast on boundary separation included zero (`r eff("m2_bs_hard_minus_easy_x_high")`; @supptbl-m2-interactions). Under high physical effort, boundary separation changed by `r pct_s("bs")`, with the whole posterior inside the ROPE (`r fmt_rope("bs")`), and the starting point did not change (`r eff("bias", rope = TRUE)`).

Under high physical effort, observed accuracy was lower on Hard trials (High − Low: `r acc_s("acc_high_low_Hard")`). It was slightly, but not significantly, higher on Identical trials (`r acc_s("acc_high_low_Standard")`) and unchanged on Easy trials (`r acc_s("acc_high_low_Easy")`; @supptbl-acc-contrasts).

## 3.2 Robustness of the physical effort effects {.unnumbered}

The drift criterion shift was unchanged when the physical effort effects were allowed to vary across participants (M4r: `r eff("crit_M4r")`). The between-participant SD of that effect was small (`r est_s("sd_effort_M4r")`). The shift was also stable at RT cutoffs of 0.15 s (`r eff("crit_thr015")`) and 0.25 s (`r eff("crit_thr025")`). Excluding the `r v("n_subchance_excluded")` participants with near-chance accuracy left the point estimate unchanged. With *N* = `r v("n_subchance_remaining")`, however, the interval included zero (`r eff("crit_subchance")`). When physical effort effects were allowed to differ by task (M4b), the criterion shift was larger in the ADT (`r eff("crit_ADT_M4b")`) than in the VDT (`r eff("crit_VDT_M4b")`), but the task difference was uncertain (`r eff("m4b_effort_x_task")`). The evidence-quality term was close to zero in every variant. The boundary effect was positive at the 0.25-s cutoff (`r eff("bs_thr025", pct = TRUE)`) and after the near-chance exclusion (`r eff("bs_subchance", pct = TRUE)`), but at the 0.15-s cutoff its interval included zero (`r eff("bs_thr015", pct = TRUE)`; @supptbl-robustness).

## 3.3 Pupil-linked decision dynamics {.unnumbered}

**Physical effort and pupil size.** High physical effort increased pupil size during the grip in the ADT (`r pt_s("grip_high_low_ADT")`), and the difference was not reliable in the VDT (`r pt_s("grip_high_low_VDT")`). Relative to the pre-probe baseline, the TEPR was smaller under high physical effort in both tasks (ADT: `r pt_s("tepr_high_low_ADT_B1")`; VDT: `r pt_s("tepr_high_low_VDT_B1")`). Relative to the pre-squeeze baseline, it did not differ between physical effort levels (ADT: `r pt_s("tepr_high_low_ADT_B0")`; VDT: `r pt_s("tepr_high_low_VDT_B0")`; @supptbl-pupil-descriptives; @suppfig-tepr). In the pupil sample, boundary separation was wider under high physical effort (`r eff("P0_bs", pct = TRUE)`), and the drift criterion shift had the same sign as in the full sample, with an interval that included zero (`r eff("P0_crit")`).

**Pupil predictors of decision parameters.** Boundary separation changed by `r pct_s("P3_bs")` per within-person SD of the TEPR, and adding the TEPR improved out-of-sample prediction (`r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P3_vs_P0")`; @fig-pupil-boundary; @tbl-pupil-ordering). TEPR did not predict the starting point (`r eff("P1_bias")`, `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P1_vs_P0")`) or drift (TEPR: `r eff("P2_drift_tepr")`; TEPR × stimulus: `r eff("P2_drift_tepr_x_stim")`; `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P2_vs_P0")`; @supptbl-pupil-models).

**Timing of the TEPR–boundary association.** TEPR correlated with RT within participants (`r fmt_r(v("tepr_rt_r", "r"), v("tepr_rt_r", "lo"), v("tepr_rt_r", "hi"))`). After the slowest 20% of trials in each participant and task were removed, boundary separation changed by `r pct_s("P3_rt_bs")` per SD of the TEPR, and the predictive gain was less than twice its standard error (`r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P3rt_vs_P0rt")`). Pupil size in the 0.5 s before the response was associated with wider boundaries and improved prediction (`r pct_s("P7_bs")`, `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P7_vs_P0pre")`). The measures taken before the decision did not predict boundary separation: previous-trial TEPR (`r pct_s("P6_bs")`, `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P6_vs_P0lag")`), pre-squeeze baseline pupil (`r pct_s("P5_bs")`, `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P5_vs_P0base")`) and grip-period pupil (`r pct_s("P8_bs")`, `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P8_vs_P0grip")`). The pre-squeeze baseline did not predict the starting point either (`r eff("P4_bias_base")`, `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P4_vs_P0base")`).

## 3.4 Model adequacy {.unnumbered}

The primary model reproduced the observed choice proportions in `r v("ppc_choice_inside_M4")` of 12 condition cells (@supptbl-ppc-choice). Of the observed RT quantiles, `r fmt_num(v("ppc_rt_inside_pct_M4"), 1)`% fell inside the 95% predictive intervals, and observed median RTs were on average `r fmt_int(v("ppc_rt_median_bias_ms_M4"))` ms slower than predicted (@suppfig-ppc). The discrepancy was largest for minority responses ("different" on Identical trials, "same" on Easy trials and "different" on Hard trials), which were slower than predicted. After moment matching and exact refits (@sec-supp-spec), no observation in any compared model had a Pareto *k* above 0.7. Non-decision time changed with the RT cutoff: `r fmt_num(v("t0_thr015", "median"), 3)` s, `r fmt_num(v("t0_M4", "median"), 3)` s and `r fmt_num(v("t0_thr025", "median"), 3)` s at cutoffs of 0.15 s, 0.20 s and 0.25 s.

# 4 Discussion {.unnumbered}

We asked whether concurrent physical effort changes how older adults make perceptual decisions by reducing the quality of the evidence they accumulate (the capacity account) or by changing how they use that evidence (the policy account). In the primary model, high physical effort did not reduce evidence quality. Instead, it shifted drift toward "same" on all trials. That shift appeared as an accuracy cost on Hard trials and, if anything, a small gain on Identical trials. The change in boundary separation was inside the region of practical equivalence, and the starting point was unchanged. High physical effort enlarged the pupil only weakly during the grip. In the pupil sample, trials with larger pupil responses during the decision had wider boundaries, whereas no pupil measure taken before the decision predicted boundary separation.

## 4.1 Evidence quality and the capacity account {.unnumbered}

The capacity account made two predictions: high physical effort should reduce evidence quality, and this loss should be largest on the hardest trials [@kahneman1973attention; @wickens2008]. The physical effort × stimulus term, which measures evidence quality, was close to zero, and its interval allowed a small decline but not a large one. In the model that let the physical effort effects vary with task difficulty, physical effort lowered drift more on Hard than on Easy trials, but that contrast only just excluded zero, and the model did not predict better than the model without the interaction (`r elpd_s("delta_elpd_M2_vs_M1", "se_delta_elpd_M2_vs_M1")`; @supptbl-model-comparison; @supptbl-m2-interactions). The data therefore leave room for a small capacity cost on the hardest discriminations, in addition to the criterion shift.

The main physical effort effect was a shift common to all trials. In diffusion-model terms, this is a change in the drift criterion: the reference point against which evidence is evaluated as favoring one response or the other [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. Because the upper boundary was "different," the criterion shift lowers drift on trials with a different probe, so those trials more often end in "same." On Identical trials the same shift moves drift further toward the correct response. The accuracy pattern follows from this. The Hard-trial cost is the change that a capacity account would predict, but here it arises mainly from a change in the criterion rather than a loss of evidence quality. Accuracy alone cannot separate the two, because Hard trials were the trials on which the shift was most consequential.

## 4.2 The criterion shift {.unnumbered}

These results agree with the earlier chapters in direction. In younger adults, task difficulty and physical effort did not interact on any measure [Chapter 1, @dastgheib_inpress_effects], and in the present sample, psychometric functions showed that high physical effort lowered "different" responses without reducing sensitivity. The reduction on Identical trials was similar in size but uncertain on its own (Chapter 2). The diffusion model places that shift in the drift criterion and adds the hint of a small additional cost on the hardest trials, which Chapter 1 did not detect. Because this chapter has no younger comparison group, and Chapter 1 used a laboratory setting and different stimulus offsets, the data cannot show whether that cost is specific to older adults.

Within the policy account, wider boundaries under high physical effort would indicate that participants protected accuracy, and narrower boundaries that they ended effortful trials sooner. Neither occurred: the estimated change was positive but practically negligible, and its interval included zero at the shortest RT cutoff. The starting point was also unchanged, so physical effort did not bias either response before the stimulus appeared. The results therefore fit the policy account, but through the drift criterion rather than through boundary separation or the starting point.

Why high physical effort would shift the criterion is not settled by these data. Chapter 2 considers three explanations: a more conservative decision policy under a concurrent demand, a change in decision processing linked to the pupil, and a bias tied to the finger used for each response. The pupil results (Section 4.4) do not support the second, because no pupil measure taken before the decision predicted the decision parameters. The response mapping (Section 4.5) leaves the third open.

## 4.3 Physical effort and pupil size {.unnumbered}

High physical effort increased pupil size during the grip in the ADT, as expected from the pupil's sensitivity to physical effort [@zenon2014pupil]; in the VDT the difference had the same sign but was not reliable. When both tasks were analyzed together with participant-specific physical effort effects (Chapter 2), the grip-period difference was not reliable, so the effect of physical effort on pupil size during the grip was weak. After the probe, the pupil rose less under high physical effort from its level before the probe, but pupil size after the probe, measured from before the squeeze, did not differ between physical effort levels. The smaller response under high physical effort therefore reflects the higher level from which the pupil rose, not a smaller pupil after the probe, which is why the choice of baseline matters for physical effort comparisons [@mathot2018]. The release of the grip, and the color change that cued it, also fall inside the TEPR window, and releasing a grip held at high physical effort differs from releasing one held at low physical effort.

One interpretation of pupil changes with physical effort comes from adaptive gain theory, which links pupil size to activity of the locus coeruleus–noradrenaline system [@astonjones2005; @joshi2016]. Isometric handgrip engages this system [@mather2020isometric], and the locus coeruleus is vulnerable in aging [@mather2016locus]. This study did not manipulate locus coeruleus activity, and the neuroimaging measures of that activity are not analyzed here. Pupil size also covaries with activity outside the locus coeruleus [@joshi2016].

## 4.4 Pupil size and boundary separation {.unnumbered}

Of the pupil measures, trial-wise TEPR had the strongest association with boundary separation, which parallels work in which larger pupil dilation on high-conflict choices predicted wider boundaries [@cavanagh2014]. Two results limit how far the association can be read as the pupil response setting the boundary. First, the TEPR window overlapped the response, TEPR correlated with RT within participants, and when the slowest trials were removed the association was about half as large and its predictive gain was no longer clearly above its standard error. A wider boundary lengthens the decision, and a longer decision lets more of the pupil response accumulate in the window. Second, none of the measures taken before the decision (the pre-squeeze baseline, the grip-period pupil and the previous trial's TEPR) predicted boundary separation.

Pupil size in the 0.5 s before the response did predict wider boundaries, so the association is not confined to processing after the response. Because that window was placed relative to the response, however, it sampled later points of the pupil response on longer decisions, so it cannot separate a pupil change that set the boundary from one that accompanied a longer decision. Taken together, pupil size tracked the decision as it unfolded, not a state measured before it. A window fixed to the probe and ending before the earliest response would separate the two, but in this design the 0.35 s between probe onset and the response cue is too short for the pupil response to develop [@mathot2018].

## 4.5 Limitations and future directions {.unnumbered}

**Boundary terms.** Boundary separation was allowed to vary with stimulus type, although stimulus types were intermixed and could not be anticipated. These terms let the model absorb RT differences between stimulus types that a diffusion model without across-trial variability cannot otherwise capture. This was most evident for minority responses, which were slower than predicted. That slow-error pattern is the signature of variability in drift across trials [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. The physical effort contrasts were stable across model variants and RT cutoffs, but absolute parameter values depend on this choice. Models with across-trial variability in drift and non-decision time [@ratcliff2002estimating] would test whether the physical effort effects survive a better account of RT distributions.

**Delayed-response design.** Because participants waited for a cue, non-decision time absorbed the enforced delay and changed almost one-for-one with the RT cutoff. It cannot be interpreted as encoding or motor time, and physical effort effects on it were not tested. The design also limits how much RT information constrains boundary separation. A free-response version of the task would test the boundary results more directly.

**Pupil sample and measure.** The pupil analyses used `r v("n_pupil_final_subjects")` of the `r v("n_final")` participants, selected on recording quality, and they are correlational at the level of trials. In that sample, the physical effort effects on the drift criterion and boundary separation had the same sign as in the full sample. The TEPR window included post-decision processing. In addition, the pre-probe baseline began shortly after the standard and so included the onset of the pupil response to it; the TEPR therefore measures the response to the probe on top of a still-rising response to the standard. The grip-period measure combined dilation related to physical effort with trial-to-trial variation in the force produced. Entering the recorded trial-wise grip force as a covariate would separate the two.

**Design.** With only two levels of physical effort, the study cannot test non-monotonic effects. Hard trials were answered incorrectly more often than correctly, so Hard-trial estimates reflect a strong bias toward "same" as well as low evidence quality. When participants with near-chance accuracy were excluded, the criterion shift kept its size, but its interval included zero. The effect is small and should be replicated.

**Response mapping.** "Different" was always given with the right index finger and "same" with the right middle finger, while the left hand held the grip. A bias acting on the evidence for one response therefore cannot be separated from the finger that gave that response; counterbalancing the mapping across participants would separate them.

**Physiological measures.** Pupil size is the only physiological measure reported here. Neuroimaging was collected during the task, including locus coeruleus activity, but those measures are outside the scope of this dissertation. Links between the pupil results and the noradrenergic system therefore remain interpretive.

**Setting.** Data were collected in an MRI scanner, which constrains luminance, posture and noise, so pupil responses and grip performance may differ from those in a laboratory.

## 4.6 Conclusion {.unnumbered}

In older adults, holding a 40% MVC grip during an auditory or visual same–different judgment shifted the drift criterion toward "same." It did not reduce the overall quality of the evidence accumulated or meaningfully change boundary separation. Pupil responses during the decision were larger on trials with wider boundaries, but pupil size measured before the decision did not predict boundary separation. Under high physical effort, older adults were therefore less likely to report a difference, a cost that falls on the small differences that are hardest to detect.

## Model specification and estimation {#sec-supp-spec .unnumbered}

The primary model (M4) was selected from nested models that differed in how physical effort, stimulus type and task entered drift and boundary separation (@supptbl-formulas). M0 had no physical effort terms on drift or boundary separation. M1 added physical effort to both, and M2 let those effects vary with task difficulty. M3 instead added the physical effort × stimulus term to drift in M1, and M4 also let drift and boundary separation differ between tasks. Allowing drift and boundary separation to differ between tasks improved out-of-sample prediction (M4 vs. M3: `r elpd_s("delta_elpd_M3_vs_M4", "se_delta_elpd_M3_vs_M4", flip = TRUE)`), whereas allowing the physical effort effects to differ between tasks did not (M4b vs. M4: `r elpd_s("delta_elpd_M4b_vs_M4", "se_delta_elpd_M4b_vs_M4")`; @supptbl-model-comparison). Two variants of M4 tested the robustness of its physical effort effects: M4b added physical effort × task interactions on drift, and M4r added by-participant random slopes for physical effort on drift and boundary separation.

The starting point did not depend on stimulus type, which could not be known before the trial. Boundary separation was allowed to vary with stimulus type to absorb RT differences between stimulus types; because stimulus types were intermixed, these terms are not interpreted as strategic settings (Section 4.5). Non-decision time had no predictors because, in a delayed-response design, it mainly absorbs the delay before the cue.

The boundary-separation intercept was bounded between 0.3 and 5, and non-decision time between 0.02 s and 0.01 s below the shortest RT. Sampling used adapt_delta = `r fmt_num(v("adapt_delta"), 2)` and a maximum tree depth of `r v("max_treedepth")`. `r v("refit_models")` did not meet the convergence criterion at `r fmt_int(v("n_iter"))` iterations and were refit with `r fmt_int(v("n_iter_refit"))` iterations. In the leave-one-out comparisons, observations with Pareto *k* > 0.7 were handled with moment matching and exact refits.

For the full pupil sample, the comparison model was P0, the primary model fit to that sample, which also gave the physical effort effects in that sample (@supptbl-pupil-models). Pupil measures with their own valid-data requirement (the pre-squeeze baseline, the previous trial's TEPR, the pre-response window and the grip period), and the sample without the slowest trials, each had a baseline model fit to the same trials (@supptbl-formulas).

## Analysis provenance (dissertation only) {.unnumbered}

Pupil samples were placed on a time axis at the recorded 250-Hz sampling rate, from 3 s before squeeze onset to the end of the confidence window. Earlier internal analyses that used a time axis derived from file timestamps were discarded, because that axis compressed time and misplaced the analysis windows; no result from those analyses is reported.

:::

```{r}
#| include: false
diag_dir <- params$diag_dir
if (is.null(diag_dir) || !nzchar(diag_dir)) {
  diag_dir <- "output/diagnostics/qmd_current"
}
dir.create(file.path(proj_root, diag_dir), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
utils::write.csv(
  data.frame(call_order = seq_along(.keys_used), key = .keys_used, stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
  file.path(proj_root, diag_dir, "keys_used.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```
